title: What we heard, saw and touched
sum: The letter has no greeting, no name and no address. It begins like the Gospel of John, with "the beginning", and with a crowd of witnesses: what "we" heard, saw with our own eyes, gazed at and touched, the life that was with the Father and was made visible. The writer announces it so that the readers may share fellowship with "us", and through us with the Father and the Son, and so that joy may be full (1:1-4).

Then comes the message: God is light, and in him there is no darkness. Three claims are tested, each beginning "If we say": fellowship with God while walking in darkness, having no sin, and never having sinned. The answer is neither despair nor pretense: walk in the light, confess your sins, and the blood of Jesus makes you clean (1:5-10).
readings: Read as a reply to a split

The "we" of the eyewitnesses stands against people who had left (2:19). On this reading, which the letter does not state outright, the "if we say" lines quote what those people claimed: that they knew God and were beyond sin, and the touched, visible Jesus answers a teaching that played down his flesh (4:2).
Read as a sermon on fellowship
Without the background of controversy the chapter is a plain call to every reader: share the life of the apostles' witness, walk honestly in the light, and do not pretend about sin.

views.H: The opening sets out the evidence before any argument: eyewitness testimony to a Jesus who could be heard, seen and touched. In the setting of a church split over who Jesus was, that is the ground on which everything else stands.
views.C: The prologue is close to the Gospel's (John 1:1-18) in words and ideas, and most scholars agree that one borrows directly from the other, though there is no consensus that the same person wrote both. Whether the letter's "we" are eyewitnesses or the keepers of their tradition is part of the authorship question.
views.L: One very long Greek sentence (1:1-3) piles up relative clauses ("what ... what ... what") before the main verb arrives. Then three "if we say" lines (1:6, 8, 10) alternate with two "if we" answers (1:7, 9): a pattern of false claim and true response that the letter will use again.
views.J: Light and darkness, truth and falsehood, walking in the way: all are the language of Israel's Scriptures and of the Dead Sea Scrolls. Confession of sin recalls the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:21) and the Psalms (Psalm 32:5), and "make clean" is the Torah's word (Leviticus 16:30).
views.T: The church has used 1:8-10 against perfectionism (Augustine against the Pelagians) and 1:9 for both private confession to God (Calvin) and the practice of confession in the church. The Catholic Catechism quotes 1:8-9 together on mercy and sin (paragraph 1847).

deep.b:
Both open with "beginning" (John 1:1, "In the beginning"; 1 John 1:1, "from the beginning"). Both speak of the Word (logos), of life, and of light (John 1:4-5; 1 John 1:2, 5). Both say the eternal one was "with" God or the Father (pros, John 1:1; 1 John 1:2). Both speak of seeing: "We gazed at his glory" (John 1:14) and "what we gazed at and our hands touched" (1:1), with the same verb.

The differences matter too. The Gospel's prologue tells a story, from creation to the Word becoming flesh. The letter's prologue gives testimony: it stacks up the senses of sight, hearing and touch, as if answering someone who doubted that the life had been physical. The Gospel says "the Word"; the letter says "the word of life" and quickly turns to "the life". Readers who think the letter was written after the Gospel see it as applying the Gospel to a church in crisis; those who think it came first see the Gospel's prologue as a fuller development of the same ideas.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the three "if we say" lines answer one claim
deep.b:
The three claims of 1:6, 1:8 and 1:10 may not be three separate errors but three steps of one: "we have fellowship with him" (1:6), so "we have no sin" now (1:8), and in fact "we have not sinned" at all (1:10). Each answer goes deeper: lying about how we live, then deceiving ourselves, then making God a liar. If so, the writer is answering a teaching that began with a high spiritual claim and ended by denying the need for the cleansing blood (1:7) and the atoning sacrifice (2:2), which would explain why the next verses go straight to the Advocate.

This is Claude's reading of the passage's shape; the idea that the "if we say" lines quote the opponents is common in the commentaries, but the three-step chain is offered here as a suggestion.

echoes: John 1:1-18; John 3:19-21; John 8:12; John 16:24; John 21:24; Leviticus 16:21, 30; Psalm 32:5; Proverbs 28:13; Luke 24:39

settings.what: The opening: testimony about the word of life
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To ground everything that follows in eyewitness testimony to a Jesus who was heard, seen and touched, before the letter deals with people who had left (2:19) and with every spirit that does not confess Jesus "as having come in the flesh" (4:2-3). It invites the readers to stay in fellowship with the witnesses, because that fellowship is fellowship with the Father and the Son. Knowing the split behind the letter turns these warm lines into a line drawn in the sand.
views: The writer was one of those who knew Jesus, the traditional view (Irenaeus and later writers name the apostle John).
The "we" are the leaders of the community that preserved the eyewitness tradition, speaking for it against those who left.

settings.what: God is light: walking in the light and dealing with sin
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To test three claims ("If we say") that may echo the teaching of those who left: fellowship with God without walking in the light, and freedom from sin. The writer keeps two things together for the readers: sin is real and must be confessed, and it is fully dealt with by Jesus' blood, his work as Advocate and his atoning sacrifice. The readers are protected both from pretending they do not sin and from despairing when they do.

title: An Advocate, a new command, and the last hour
sum: The writer turns to "my little children". He writes so that they will not sin, but if they do, they have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for their sins and for the whole world (2:1-2). Knowing God shows in keeping his commands, above all the command to love, old and new at once, for the darkness is passing and the real light already shines (2:3-11). He writes to children, fathers and young men, and warns them not to love the world, which is passing away (2:12-17).

Then the crisis comes into the open. It is the last hour: many antichrists have appeared, and they came from inside the church. "They went out from among us." The liar is the one who denies that Jesus is the Messiah, and so denies the Father and the Son. But the readers have an anointing from the Holy One, and they all know the truth; they need only remain in what they heard from the beginning (2:18-27). The chapter ends with the call to remain in him, so as to stand unashamed at his coming (2:28-29).
readings: Read as a church in crisis

Verses 18-27 are the center: a group has left, claiming a truer knowledge. The tests of 2:3-11 (obedience and love) and the reassurance of 2:12-14 and 2:20-27 are aimed at people shaken by their departure.
Read as teaching for any church

Read on its own, the chapter is a guide to Christian life: forgiveness through Christ, obedience shown in love, a warning against worldly desire, and faithfulness to the original gospel when new teachers arrive.

views.H: The opponents, the "antichrists" of 2:18-22, had been members. The letter's "they went out" (2:19) and the warnings about "the people who are leading you astray" (2:26) are the main evidence for the split.
views.C: Scholars debate whether the opponents denied the Jewish claim that Jesus is the Messiah, or taught a split between the man Jesus and the heavenly Christ (as Irenaeus reports of Cerinthus), or a docetic Christ without a real body. The change from "I am writing" to "I have written" in 2:12-14 is also debated.
views.L: The chapter weaves its threads: light and darkness (2:8-11), the world and its craving (2:15-17), truth and lie (2:21-22), and the key verb "remain" (2:6, 10, 14, 17, 19, 24, 27, 28). The wordplay of Christos, antichristos and chrisma (2:18-27) runs under the surface.
views.J: Some read the Advocate and the atoning sacrifice against the Day of Atonement, which the Greek Old Testament calls the day of hilasmos (Leviticus 25:9). Many hear in the "old command" the love command of Leviticus 19:18, though the letter itself calls it the word the readers heard "from the beginning" (2:7). The promise that no one needs to teach his neighbor recalls Jeremiah 31:34. Denying that Jesus is the Messiah was the line between synagogue and church in John's Gospel (John 9:22).
views.T: 2:2 became a key text in the debate over the extent of the atonement (see the card). 2:19 is used in the debate over whether true believers can fall away. 2:20 and 2:27 have been read of the Spirit's anointing, and the Orthodox Church connects them with chrismation.

deep.b:
1 John gives only a few clues: they had been members (2:19); the letter calls the one who denies "that Jesus is the Messiah" the liar and the antichrist (2:22); every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God (4:2-3); they were in the world, and the world listened to them (4:5); and the letter insists that Jesus came "not in the water only, but in the water and in the blood" (5:6).

Scholars have offered several reconstructions; the letter itself names no school. (1) Docetists, who held that Christ only seemed to have a body. Early in the second century Ignatius of Antioch wrote against those who said that Christ "only seemed to suffer" (To the Smyrnaeans 2), and Polycarp turned this letter's own words on such teachers: "For whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist" (Philippians 7). (2) A teaching like that of Cerinthus, whom Irenaeus describes as saying that "after his baptism, Christ descended upon him in the form of a dove" and that "at last Christ departed from Jesus" before the passion (Against Heresies 1.26.1). Irenaeus quotes 2:18-22 against the systems "which divide the Lord" (3.16.5), and tells the story of John fleeing a bath-house at Ephesus because "Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is within" (3.3.4). (3) Secessionists from John's own circle. Raymond Brown argued that both sides knew the teaching found in the Fourth Gospel and "interpret it differently" (The Community of the Beloved Disciple, 1979), dividing over Christ, ethics, the last things and the Spirit; Peter Leithart notes that Brown found it implausible that they were Jews who denied that Jesus was the Messiah. Brown's history of a "Johannine community" has been challenged since (Richard Bauckham in 2007, Adele Reinhartz, Robert Kysar, Hugo Méndez). (4) Jewish believers going back to Judaism. Terry Griffith reads 2:22 as "The Messiah is Jesus" and argues that "it is the messiahship of Jesus that is in question": on his reading 4:2 says the same thing, and the closing warning against idols (5:21) turns Judaism's own polemic against idols back on it (Tyndale Bulletin 48.1, 1997). The first two views fit the stress on flesh and blood; the last fits 2:22 and the conflicts of John's Gospel (John 9:22).

The letter never sets out their teaching, and this restraint is itself a lesson: it answers by pointing to Jesus and to love, not by describing the error in detail.

2:2 has stood at the center of a long argument about whom Christ died for. Those who hold that Christ died for every person read "the whole world" in its plain wide sense. The Remonstrants' second article (1610) says that Jesus Christ "died for all men and for every man" and quotes this verse, while adding "that no one actually enjoys this forgiveness of sins except the believer". The General Baptists' Standard Confession (1660) quotes it too. Calvin, who accepted that Christ "suffered sufficiently for the whole world, but efficiently only for the elect" as a true statement, said it was not the point of this verse: John "does not include the reprobate, but designates those who should believe". The Synod of Dort (1618-1619) answered the Remonstrants: Christ's death is "more than sufficient to atone for the sins of the whole world", but its saving effectiveness works itself out "in all the elect". The Amyraldians, a Reformed school, put God's decree of an atonement "for all alike if they believe" before his decree of election. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and Methodist documents teach that Christ died for all. See the card below.

echoes: John 13:33-35; John 14:15-17, 26; John 12:35; John 17:15; Leviticus 19:18; Jeremiah 31:34; Romans 3:25; 2 Thessalonians 2:3; Mark 13:22; Genesis 3:6

settings.what: Knowing him means keeping his commands
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To give the readers a test they can see: anyone who claims to know God, to remain in him, or to be in the light shows it by keeping his commands, above all by loving his brother. If the opponents claimed a special knowledge of God while despising the church they had left, this test exposes the claim. For the readers it is also a comfort: their love for each other is evidence that the light is shining in them.

settings.what: Why I am writing; do not love the world
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: The whole church, addressed as "little children" and as "fathers" and "young men"
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To reassure the readers before the warnings: their sins are forgiven, they know the Father and the one from the beginning, and they have already won the victory over the evil one. Then to warn them against the world's cravings and display of wealth, which are passing away. Readers shaken by the split hear that they are not on the losing side.
views: Real age groups in the church: children, older men, younger men.
New believers, mature believers, and those in the thick of the struggle.
All readers are "little children"; within them, older and younger.

settings.what: The last hour: the antichrists and the anointing
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To explain the departure of a group from the church as a sign of the last hour, to name their teaching (denying that Jesus is the Messiah, and so the Father and the Son) and to assure the readers that they do not need the departed teachers' instruction: they have an anointing from the Holy One and the message they heard from the beginning. This changes the reading of the chapter: it is not abstract teaching on the end times but pastoral care for a wounded church.
views: The opponents split the heavenly Christ from the man Jesus or denied his real flesh (4:2; 5:6).
The opponents had returned to the synagogue and denied that Jesus is the Messiah (2:22).

settings.what: God's children and the devil's children
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To lift the readers' eyes to Christ's coming and to what they already are, God's children, and to draw the consequence: those born from God do righteousness and do not sin, while those who commit sin show themselves the devil's children. The readers, troubled by the opponents' claims, learn to judge by fruit, and learn that being God's child is the ground of their hope (3:2-3).

traditions.q: Did Christ die for the sins of every person, or for the elect (2:2)?
views: Christ died for all without exception. The Catechism says, "There is not, never has been, and never will be a single human being for whom Christ did not suffer", citing the Council of Quiercy (853) and 1 John 2:2 (paragraph 605), and it quotes this verse again for the sacrifice "for the sins of the whole world" (paragraph 606).

The Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), written to refute the Calvinist teaching of Cyril Lucaris, says that Christ, "in giving Himself a ransom for all", made "a reconciliation between God and man" (decree 8), and rejects as a defamation of God the teaching that "the Divine Will is thus solely and without cause the author of their condemnation" (decree 3). It does not cite this verse.

The Formula of Concord teaches that "the promise of the Gospel is universalis (universal), that is, it pertains to all men", and cites this verse: "His blood is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 1:7; 2:2" (Solid Declaration 11.28).

The Canons of Dort teach that Christ's death is "more than sufficient to atone for the sins of the whole world" (second main point, article 3), but that God willed its "saving effectiveness" to "work itself out in all the elect" (article 8). Calvin, commenting on this verse, said John "does not include the reprobate, but designates those who should believe". A Reformed minority, the Amyraldians (after Moses Amyraut of Saumur), also called hypothetical universalists, taught that God decreed Christ's atonement "for all alike if they believe" before his decree of election.
Article 31 of the Thirty-Nine Articles calls the offering of Christ "that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction" "for all the sins of the whole world, both original and actual".
Wesley read the verse universally: "Just as wide as sin extends, the propitiation extends also" (Explanatory Notes on 2:2).

Baptists are divided. Particular Baptists, in the tradition of the Second London Confession (1689), hold that "To all those for whom Christ has obtained eternal redemption, He does certainly and effectually apply and communicate the same" (chapter 8, paragraph 8), so the redemption is particular. The General Baptists' Standard Confession (1660) says Christ "as freely gave himself a ransome for all", "tasting death for every man", and quotes this verse: "a propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole World" (article 3).

title: Born from God
sum: "Look what sort of love the Father has given us": believers are called God's children, and they are. What they will be is not yet visible, but when he appears they will be like him, for they will see him as he is (3:1-3). Then come the hardest sentences of the letter: everyone who remains in him "does not sin"; the one born from God "cannot sin", because God's seed remains in him. The one who commits sin is from the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son of God appeared to undo the devil's works (3:4-10).

The second half turns to love. The message from the beginning is to love each other, not like Cain, who slaughtered his brother. Hatred is murder; love is laying down one's life, as he laid down his for us, and it shows in sharing what one has with a brother in need. Even when our heart accuses us, God is greater than our heart. His command is one: believe the name of his Son and love each other. And the Spirit he has given is how we know he remains in us (3:11-24).
readings: Read as a call to holiness
3:6-9 states what God's children are: people whose new birth makes sin foreign to them. The chapter asks readers to live up to what they are, and in love above all.
Read as a test of the opponents

Those who claimed to be beyond sin (1:8) but did not love the brothers they had left are shown by their fruit to be "from the devil" (3:8-10), like Cain. The chapter reassures those who stayed and love one another.

views.H: In a church split by people who claimed spiritual superiority, the letter defines the true children of God by two marks: doing righteousness and loving the brothers. Sharing goods with the needy (3:17) was a practical test in small house churches.
views.C: The tension between 1:8-10 and 3:6-9 is one of the hardest problems in the letter. Readers have explained it in several ways (see the deep dive).
views.L: The chapter is built on contrasts: God's children and the devil's, righteousness and sin, love and hate, Cain and Abel, death and life. "From the beginning" (3:8, 11) ties the devil's sinning and the message of love to the start of the human story.
views.J: Cain (Genesis 4) is the Bible's first murderer, and later Jewish tradition gave him an angelic father: the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 4:1 speaks of "the Angel", and Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 21 names Sammael. The Torah already forbids hating one's brother (Leviticus 19:17) and closing one's hand to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7). The verb of 3:3, "makes himself pure" (hagnizei heauton), is the one John's Gospel uses for the pilgrims who came to Jerusalem before the Passover "to make themselves pure" (John 11:55).
views.T: 3:6-9 is the classic text of the debate over Christian perfection: Wesley's teaching, Lutheran and Reformed teaching that the believer remains a sinner, and Catholic teaching on venial sin. 3:2 is a key verse for the beatific vision (Catholic) and theosis (Orthodox).

deep.h: "Does not sin" (3:6-9) and "If we say we have no sin" (1:8-10)
deep.b:
The letter says both that "If we say, 'We have no sin,' we are leading ourselves astray" (1:8) and that "Everyone who has been born from God does not commit sin ... He cannot sin" (3:9; compare 5:18). It even writes "so that you not sin" and then provides for those who do (2:1). Several solutions have been offered.

(1) The tense. Greek present tenses can describe ongoing action, so many translations write "keep on sinning" or "make a practice of sinning" in 3:6-9. The believer sins (1:8) but does not live in sin. The objection: the same present tense is used of believers who sin in 5:16, and the Greek words alone do not carry "keep on". This site therefore keeps "does not sin" and explains the readings.

(2) A particular sin. The sin the believer "does not" commit is the "sin headed toward death" (5:16), apostasy or the denial of Christ, or the end-time "lawlessness" of 3:4. The ordinary sins of 1:8-10 are another matter.

(3) The new nature. 3:9 describes what the child of God is by birth; 1:8 describes what he still does. Calvin: "the Spirit of God restrains the lusting of sin". Luther set 3:9 and 1:8 side by side and said that both are true (Smalcald Articles 3.3.45).

(4) Christian perfection. John Wesley took the words at their plain value: "There is no such word in the text" as "habitually", and "A Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin" (Sermon 40, Christian Perfection, II.6, II.20). He read 1:8 by 1:10 ("the tenth verse fixes the sense of the eighth") and defined sin as a willful breaking of a known law; "sin, improperly so called", involuntary mistakes, still "needs the atoning blood", and "sinless perfection is a phrase I never use" (A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, section 19).

(5) The ideal and the real. The letter states the ideal of the new age (3:2) and the present reality side by side, and leaves the tension standing on purpose: the believer is called to what he already is.

deep.title: Claude's theory: "from the beginning" in 3:8 and 3:11
deep.b:
The phrase "from the beginning" comes twice in this chapter in quick succession: "the devil has been sinning from the beginning" (3:8) and "the message you heard from the beginning ... we are to love each other" (3:11). Then comes Cain (3:12), the first story after the garden. The writer may be setting two beginnings side by side: the beginning of the gospel in the readers' lives, where they heard the command to love, and the beginning of human history, where the first brothers ended in murder. The readers stand at a new beginning that undoes the old one (3:8, "to undo the works of the devil").

This is Claude's suggestion. That 1 John uses "from the beginning" in more than one sense is widely noted; the link between the two uses here and Genesis 4 is offered as a theory.

echoes: John 1:12-13, 29; John 3:3-8; John 5:24; John 8:44; John 10:11; John 15:12-13; Genesis 4:1-16; Leviticus 19:17; Deuteronomy 15:7; Matthew 5:21-22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3; Jude 1:11

settings.what: Love each other: Cain, the cross and the needy brother
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To make love practical and costly: not like Cain, who hated his brother, but like Christ, who laid down his life. For readers in small churches, the test is whether those who have enough share with a brother in need. The section also comforts those whose consciences accuse them: God is greater than our heart. Knowing that the opponents had walked away from their brothers sharpens the point: leaving the fellowship was itself a failure of love.

traditions.q: Can a Christian stop sinning in this life (3:6-9; compare 1:8)?
views: The Council of Trent does not cite these verses, but it answers the question they raise. It taught that the just "at times fall into at least light and daily sins, which are also called venial", yet "not therefore do they cease to be just" (session 6, chapter 11), and it condemned the claim that a person can avoid all venial sins through life "except by a special privilege from God, as the Church holds in regard of the Blessed Virgin" (canon 23).

Luther held both verses true: the one born of God does not let sin rule, for "If sin does what it wants, the Holy Spirit and faith are not present", yet he set 1:8 beside 3:9 and said that it "is also true" that believers still have sin (Smalcald Articles 3.3.44-45).

Sanctification is "throughout, in the whole man; yet imperfect in this life, there abiding still some remnants of corruption in every part; whence ariseth a continual and irreconcilable war" (Westminster Confession 13.2). Calvin read 3:9 as the Spirit restraining sin so that believers "constantly cleave to righteousness", not as freedom from all sin.

Article 15 of the Thirty-Nine Articles quotes 1:8: "But all we the rest, although baptized, and born again in Christ, yet offend in many things; and if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Article 16 adds that "After we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin", and condemns those "which say, they can no more sin as long as they live here".

Yes, in Wesley's sense. Wesley taught that "A Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin", reading 3:9 without adding "habitually" ("There is no such word in the text"). He meant willful sin against a known law; involuntary mistakes remain and still need the atoning blood, and he never used the phrase "sinless perfection".

The Second London Confession (1689), in words close to Westminster's, says: "This sanctification is throughout the whole man, yet imperfect in this life; there abides still some remnants of corruption" (chapter 13, paragraph 2).

title: Test the spirits; God is love
sum: Not every spirit is to be trusted. Many false prophets have gone out into the world, and the test is what they confess: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God; every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not. The readers have won the victory over them, because the one in them is greater than the one in the world (4:1-6).

Then the letter reaches its summit: "God is love." Love comes from God; everyone who loves has been born from God. God's love was made visible when he sent his only Son into the world, as the atoning sacrifice where our sins are concerned. No one has ever gazed at God, but if we love each other, God remains in us. Complete love throws out fear, for fear has to do with punishment. We love because he loved us first, and no one can love the unseen God while hating the brother he can see (4:7-21).
readings: Read as doctrine and ethics joined

The chapter refuses to separate right belief (4:1-6) from right love (4:7-21): the God who is love showed it by sending the Son in the flesh, so denying the flesh and failing to love are two sides of one error.
Read as a meditation on love
Many readers come to 4:7-21 on its own, as the New Testament's fullest statement that God is love, and as a source of comfort for those afraid of judgment (4:17-18).

views.H: Early churches heard prophets speaking by the Spirit, and wandering teachers visited from church to church (2 John 10; 3 John 5-10). The letter gives the readers a simple test for such visitors: their confession about Jesus.
views.C: The test in 4:2-3 is one of the main clues to the opponents' teaching (docetism or a split Christology). The variant "separates Jesus" (4:3), known to Irenaeus and to Socrates' "ancient copies", shows how early readers understood the error.
views.L: The chapter has two movements, testing (4:1-6) and loving (4:7-21), each with its "by this we know". "God is love" is said twice (4:8, 16), framing the sending of the Son (4:9-10), the unseen God (4:12) and the casting out of fear (4:18).
views.J: The Torah's tests of prophets (Deuteronomy 13; 18) and the Dead Sea Scrolls' "spirits of truth and falsehood" stand behind 4:1-6. "No one has ever gazed at God" recalls Exodus 33:20, and love of God and neighbor joins the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4-5) to Leviticus 19:18.
views.T: "God is love" became a central text for theology and devotion: Augustine preached on it ("Love, and do what you will"), and the Catholic Catechism says "God's very being is love" (paragraph 221). Wesley read 4:18 as excluding "slavish fear", not reverence.

deep.b:
Augustine preached ten homilies on this letter. On 4:7-8 he went so far as to say, "Love is of God: Love IS God", and he drew from it his most famous sentence: "Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will" (Homily 7.5, 7.8). He did not mean that any act is good if one feels love; he explained, "whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare": let "the root of love be within", and only good will grow from it.

John Wesley noted that God is often called holy, righteous and wise, "but not holiness, righteousness, or wisdom in the abstract", as he is here called love (Explanatory Notes on 4:8). The Catholic Catechism: "God's very being is love" (paragraph 221), quoting 4:8 and 4:16.

The letter itself guards the sentence from becoming sentimental: it defines God's love by an act, the sending of the Son "to be the atoning sacrifice where our sins are concerned" (4:10), and it makes love for the brother the test of love for God (4:20).

echoes: Deuteronomy 13:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Mark 13:22; John 1:14, 18; John 3:16; John 4:42; John 14:17; John 16:11; Exodus 33:20; Mark 12:29-31; 2 John 1:7; Revelation 2:2

settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To protect the readers from teachers and prophets who claimed to speak by the Spirit but denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. The writer gives them one clear test and the confidence that they have already won. For readers who met wandering prophets, this was a practical rule for whom to welcome and whom to refuse (compare 2 John 10).

settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To root the command to love in God's own nature and in the sending of his Son, and so to show the readers that love for each other is not one virtue among many but the sign that God remains in them. It also frees them from fear of the judgment day. After a split, this teaches the faithful to love even when love has been betrayed.

title: Faith that wins the victory
sum: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Messiah has been born from God, and loving the Father means loving his children and keeping his commands, which are not heavy. Faith is the victory that has won over the world (5:1-5). Jesus came through water and blood, not in the water only but in the water and in the blood, and the Spirit testifies. The three witnesses agree: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has the life (5:6-12).

The letter states its purpose: so that you will know that you have eternal life. It speaks of freedom in prayer, of praying for a brother who sins, and of a "sin headed toward death". It ends with three "we know" sentences, a confession that the Son "is the real God and eternal life", and a sudden last line: "Little children, guard yourselves against idols" (5:13-21).
readings: Read as the letter's conclusion

5:13 echoes the purpose of John's Gospel (John 20:31), and the closing "we know" lines gather up the letter's assurance. The abrupt warning about idols sums up everything in a word: hold to the real God.
Read as a defense of the incarnation
The water and blood (5:6) answer teachers who accepted Christ's baptism but not his death; the testimony of the Spirit, the water and the blood confirms the Jesus of the eyewitnesses (1:1-3).

views.H: "Water and blood" may answer a teaching like that of Cerinthus, that the Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross (Irenaeus). The warning about idols fits life in the cities of Asia, full of temples.
views.C: 5:7-8 holds the most famous textual addition in the New Testament, the Johannine Comma; 5:18 has a close variant ("himself" or "him") on which NA27 and NA28 differ; and 5:20 raises the question whether the letter calls Jesus "the real God".
views.L: The chapter collects the letter's key words one last time: born from God, love, commands, victory, testimony, life, know, the evil one, the real one. It closes as abruptly as it opened, without a greeting or farewell.
views.J: The three witnesses recall the Torah's rule that a matter stands on two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). The "sin headed toward death" recalls the Torah's distinction between sins done by mistake and sins done "with a high hand" (Numbers 15:27-31). The last word, idols, is the first commandment's concern.
views.T: The Johannine Comma shaped Latin and Protestant Bibles for centuries. 5:16-17 is cited by the Catholic Catechism for the distinction between mortal and venial sin, which Calvin and other Reformers rejected (see the card). 5:20 is a text in the doctrine of Christ's divinity.

deep.h: The Johannine Comma: how the "three heavenly witnesses" entered and left the Bible
deep.b:
The KJV's 1 John 5:7-8 reads: "For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth, the Spirit, and the water, and the blood: and these three agree in one." The words in heaven ... in earth are called the Johannine Comma (Latin comma, a short clause).

Latin beginnings. The first certain quotation of the words as part of the letter is in the Liber Apologeticus, a Latin work of about 380 probably by Priscillian of Ávila; Theodor Zahn called it "the earliest quotation of the passage which is certain". Earlier, Cyprian of Carthage (died 258) wrote of the Father, Son and Spirit, "And these three are one"; scholars disagree whether he knew the added words or was reading the Trinity into 5:8 (On the Unity of the Church 6). Tertullian, earlier still, wrote of the Father, Son and Spirit, "These Three are one essence, not one Person, as it is said, I and my Father are One" (Against Praxeas 25), quoting John 10:30, not this letter; he is listed among the witnesses for the shorter text. The NET Bible's judgment is that the reading "seems to have arisen in a fourth century Latin homily in which the text was allegorized to refer to members of the Trinity". The two oldest Vulgate manuscripts, Codex Fuldensis (546) and Codex Amiatinus, do not have it, though Fuldensis has a prologue that mentions it; Old Latin copies from Spain do, sometimes with the earthly witnesses first. It spread through the medieval Vulgate and was printed in the Sixtine (1590) and Clementine (1592) editions.

Greek. No Greek manuscript has the words before the 1300s. They appear in Greek first in a translation of the Acts of the Lateran Council of 1215, then in a few late manuscripts: 629 (1300s-1400s, with Greek and Latin side by side), 918 (1500s), 61 (Codex Montfortianus, about 1520, now in Trinity College, Dublin, whose wording was translated from the Latin), 2473 (1600s) and 2318 (1700s), and in later notes in the margins of a few others.

Erasmus. Two Greek New Testaments were printed in these years. The Complutensian Polyglot, a Bible in several languages sponsored by Cardinal Cisneros, printed its New Testament in 1514, with the added words in Greek and in Latin; but the pope sanctioned the work only in 1520, and it was published and distributed in 1520-1521, so Erasmus' edition reached readers first. Erasmus left the words out of his Greek New Testament of 1516 and 1519 because his Greek manuscripts lacked them. Accused of favoring Arianism, he added them in his third edition of 1522, after being told of a Greek manuscript that had them (probably Codex 61, which he called Codex Britannicus), while voicing his doubts in his notes. The popular story that he had promised to add them if a single Greek manuscript were found has been questioned: H. J. de Jonge (1980) argued that it "has no foundation in Erasmus' works", and Bruce Metzger removed it from the third edition of his textbook. Luther's German New Testament was made from Erasmus' second edition and lacked the words. The KJV translators worked mainly from Beza's Greek edition of 1598, built on Erasmus' later editions, and the KJV of 1611 printed the words.

Debate and decision. Isaac Newton wrote against the verse in a letter to John Locke in 1690, published in 1754 as An Historical Account of Two Notable Corruptions of Scripture. In the Catholic Church the Holy Office ruled on 13 January 1897 that theologians could not "with safety" deny the words' authenticity; on 2 June 1927 the question was declared open to investigation. The Nova Vulgata, the Catholic Church's official Latin Bible today, does not have them, and English Bibles made from the critical Greek text have left them out of the main text since the English Revised Version of 1881.

What it does not mean. The doctrine of the Trinity was not built on these words: the Greek fathers who defined it in the 300s, such as Athanasius, Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, never quote the added words; they are counted as witnesses to the shorter text because of that silence, which would be strange if the words had stood in their Bibles. The churches that confess the Trinity today ground it in other passages (Matthew 28:19; John 1:1; 2 Corinthians 13:14).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the three witnesses and the scene at the cross
deep.b:
John's Gospel tells that at his death Jesus "handed over his spirit" (John 19:30), that "right away blood and water came out" of his side (John 19:34), and that "The man who saw this has given testimony" (John 19:35). The same three things, spirit, water and blood, and the same word, testimony, return in 1 John 5:6-8. The letter may be pointing its readers back to that one moment at the cross as the place where all three witnesses first spoke together, and to the eyewitness of John 19:35 as the "we" of 1:1-3.

This is Claude's suggestion. Many commentators link 5:6 with John 19:34; the reading of all three witnesses, including the Spirit, as a recall of John 19:30-35 is offered here as a theory, and the Greek of John 19:30 (paredōken to pneuma, "handed over his spirit") is often read simply as a way of saying that Jesus died.

echoes: John 3:36; John 16:33; John 17:3, 15; John 19:34-35; John 20:31; Deuteronomy 19:15; Deuteronomy 30:11; Matthew 11:30; Numbers 15:27-31; Acts 5:1-11; 1 Corinthians 11:30; James 5:15-20

settings.what: Faith that wins the victory; the three witnesses
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To join believing that Jesus is the Messiah, loving God's children and keeping his commands into one life, and to ground that faith in testimony: the water and the blood of Jesus' earthly life and death, and the Spirit. For readers whose former friends accepted a spiritual Christ but not his death, the stress on "the blood" tells them which Jesus to hold on to.
views: The "water and blood" answer teachers who held that the Christ came at the baptism but did not die (Irenaeus on Cerinthus).
The verses confess the whole earthly life of Jesus, from baptism to cross, without a specific opponent in view.

settings.what: The purpose of the letter and its last words
settings.by: The writer, who does not give his name; traditionally John the apostle (see the opening pages)
settings.to: Believers in a circle of churches, traditionally in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, who had stayed after a group left them (2:19)
settings.when: Probably late in the first century (traditionally the AD 90s), soon after the split
settings.why: To tell the readers in plain words why the letter was written: so that they will know they have eternal life. It guides their prayer, including prayer for a sinning brother, sets a limit where the sin is "headed toward death", and gathers up their certainty in three "we know" sentences. The last line, a warning against idols, sends them into cities full of temples, holding to "the real God".

views: Yes. The Catechism teaches that "the distinction between mortal and venial sin, already evident in Scripture, became part of the tradition of the Church", citing these verses (paragraph 1854). "Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart of man by a grave violation of God's law"; "Venial sin allows charity to subsist, even though it offends and wounds it" (paragraph 1855).

Orthodox teachers use the words differently. The Orthodox Church in America's question-and-answer page says of the Catholic categories of mortal and venial sin, "These categories do not exist in the Orthodox Church. Sin is sin.", and reads Stanley Harakas's "There is a sin which is mortal", said with 5:16, in the sense of a deadly sin, a sin unto death. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) does speak of "mortal sins" (decrees 16 and 18).

Lutherans keep the term "mortal sin" and tie it to faith. Justifying faith, says the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, is not "an idle knowledge, neither can it coexist with mortal sin" (on article 4), and Luther wrote that when holy people "fall into manifest sins", as David did, "then faith and the Holy Spirit have left them" (Smalcald Articles 3.3.43). Neither document cites 5:16-17.

No such distinction. Calvin, on this verse: "The Apostle, however, does not here distinguish between venial and mortal sin, as it was afterwards commonly done", and "altogether foolish is that distinction which prevails under the Papacy"; the sin unto death is "apostasy, by which men wholly alienate themselves from God". The Westminster Confession: "As there is no sin so small, but it deserves damnation; so there is no sin so great, that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent" (15.4).
Article 16 of the Thirty-Nine Articles uses the term: "Not every deadly sin willingly committed after Baptism is sin against the Holy Ghost, and unpardonable."

Wesley read the sin "not unto death" as "any sin but total apostasy from both the power and form of godliness", and allowed that the sin unto death "may likewise mean, one which God has determined to punish with death" (Explanatory Notes on 5:16).
